candidates.tagline: $3.8M NZ cycleway hated by cyclists AND drivers — torn out after 16 months
candidates.story: In November 2026, New Plymouth District Council voted at an extraordinary meeting to rip out its 16-month-old $3.8M Devon Street cycleway — nicknamed 'Tim Tam Alley' for the shape of its chunky concrete lane separators — after motorists reported tyre damage and blocked driveways, some cyclists found the lane too narrow and clipped the blocks, and 7,500 residents signed a petition to remove it; demolition is expected to cost the council another $300K–$1.6M.
candidates.why_funny: The city installed a bike lane designed to protect cyclists that managed to annoy cyclists (too narrow, blocks clipped tyres), infuriate drivers (tyre damage, blocked driveways), and cost $300K more just to tear out — all within 16 months of opening.
candidates.alt: Three Tim Tam chocolate biscuit-shaped sandwich cookies — the same shape as the concrete lane dividers that gave New Plymouth's controversial Devon Street cycleway its nickname 'Tim Tam Alley', voted to be demolished after just 16 months

candidates.tagline: Apple's $1,999 foldable iPhone has a hinge that cracks its own screen
candidates.story: Apple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo ($1,999), launched October 23, 2026; within weeks owners reported a crunching hinge sound followed by a horizontal row of dead pixels on the inner screen — iFixit's teardown found the hinge's center support bar doesn't retract far enough and presses directly into the display electronics; Apple acknowledged the issue and explained its hinge assembly used 'AI algorithms' to match components, with replacement screens costing $999 out of warranty.
candidates.why_funny: Apple advertised the iPhone Duo as achieving 'a visually crease-free state' and shipped a $2,000 phone whose hinge cracks its own screen — then explained the hinge design process involved AI, as if that made it less broken.
candidates.alt: An Apple iPhone Duo foldable phone open to show its flexible inner display and distinctive book-fold hinge — the same hinge mechanism later found to press against the display electronics, cracking screens in reported units
